svg.text: Core entities + API — the nouns, then the transport that shapes the contract
pick the CONNECTION first (it decides whether the API can even exist) · then name commands, not REST resources
Core entities (bullets first, schema later)
Actor — User: all users are PEERS
no privileged actor — no Uber driver/rider split, no creator/viewer
Chat — id · name · metadata
ONE entity for 1:1 and groups — a 2-person chat is still a chat
ChatParticipant — chatId + participantId
composite PK (chatId) → "who's in this chat" ·
GSI on participantId → "which chats am I in"
Message — id · contents · senderId · timestamp
server stamps the time (consistent clocks across senders)
Inbox — recipientId · messageId
one row per UNDELIVERED copy → makes delivery provable
Client — userId + clientId (a DEVICE)
"a person isn't offline — a device is offline" (verbatim)
API — connectivity first, commands second
1 · latency-sensitive? YES (500 ms) → not polling
2 · frequent BIDIRECTIONAL traffic? YES → not SSE (one-way)
3 · P2P / media calls in scope? NO → WebSockets ✓
real WhatsApp = a plain TLS connection — same principle:
a persistent pipe ferrying messages BOTH ways
Client → server (requests):
create_chat · send_message · create_attachment
modify_participants (add / remove a member)
Server → client (pushes):
new_message · chat_created · participants_changed
no standard for describing a WS API →
name the commands, say "this is the start", iterate
Why not REST? REST cannot push server → client.
A chat API is ~half server-initiated events; plain HTTP request/response only covers the client→server half.
The new noun that surfaces here: the CLIENT — starts as "the thing that received the message",
later becomes the per-device unit of delivery (multi-device extension).
WebSockets are STATEFUL → the load-balancer story changes in deep dive 1. That's where senior candidates earn their marks.
